messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 39-year-old Salvadoran-American woman who has worked as a detective in a mid-sized urban police department for eleven years. She came to therapy after a performance review flagged her behaviour as erratic during a domestic violence callout — a category of case she had been quietly requesting reassignment from for nearly two years. She presented as guarded, composed in posture but watchful in the eyes, and she chose the chair nearest the door before the therapist had finished gesturing toward the seating.

Valentina grew up in a household where her father's rages were a weather system the whole family learned to read. The violence she witnessed was not occasional; it was seasonal, cyclical, and loud. She remembers, with the quality of a photograph rather than a film, specific images: her mother pressed against the kitchen wall, her father's shirt dark with sweat under the arms, the particular smell of him when he came home that way — sour and close and wrong. She remembers the shouting most of all, not the words but the volume, the way it seemed to occupy every room simultaneously so that there was nowhere in the apartment that was safe. She was seven the first time she wedged herself behind the sofa to wait it out. She was seventeen when she left.

She had carried these years quietly for a long time, or believed she had. The work of detecting, she had always told herself, required exactly the kind of vigilance she had spent her childhood developing. For years this felt true. Then, approximately eighteen months ago, she attended a domestic disturbance call that ended with her physically restraining a man whose body odour — that same sour, particular smell — was identical, as far as her body was concerned, to her father's. She completed the arrest. She drove home. She sat in her car for two hours and did not go inside.

Since then, the images have returned in ways she cannot control and cannot, paradoxically, summon when she tries. When she attempts to sit down and deliberately reconstruct what happened in her childhood, the memory goes slippery and inaccessible, like trying to grip something underwater. But when she is not trying — when a colleague raises his voice across the bullpen, or when someone moves suddenly in her peripheral vision in the corridor — the images arrive without invitation: static, vivid, grief-saturated. She described the grief as disproportionate and humiliating, a word she used more than once. She had come to believe that this disproportionality was evidence of something fundamentally broken in her, that her reactions since these episodes began meant she was losing her grip on her own mind.

She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning and moves through her apartment checking the locks, the windows, the door to the bedroom where her partner, Delia, is sleeping. Delia has noticed. Valentina has not explained. Physical affection between them has become rare and then rarer still; Valentina finds herself stiffening at any touch, even a hand on her shoulder, and has developed the habit of angling her body away in crowded spaces, in the elevator at work, in any situation where contact might be unavoidable. Delia has begun sleeping on her side of the bed with a careful distance between them that neither of them has named aloud.

At work, Valentina selects her seat in briefings based on sightlines to the exit. She has told herself this is professional habit, the occupational instinct of someone trained to assess environments. She is certain, at some level she does not fully examine, that she cannot trust her own judgment in high-stakes moments — that the event happened to her, that she was made for it somehow by the kind of person she is, and that this same quality in her will eventually cause her to fail someone who needs her.

What finally brought her to seek help was not the performance review but Delia asking, quietly, whether Valentina still wanted her there. Valentina said yes. She was not sure she believed herself. She came to therapy hoping to stop hurting herself during the worst nights, and afraid, more than anything, that what the therapy would find is that there is nothing left underneath the vigilance to work with.
